items.title: A thing that really annoys me about English idiom is that when people name the four cardinal directions, they tend to say "east and west" rather than "west and east" – but they tend to say "left and right" rather than "right and left". And (in the usual north-at-the-top map orientation) those are opposite ways round.
items.content:
A thing that really annoys me about English idiom is that when people name the four cardinal directions, they tend to say "east and west" rather than "west and east" – but they tend to say "left and right" rather than "right and left". And (in the usual north-at-the-top map orientation) those are opposite ways round.

I've always struggled to tell east from west. Whenever I have to translate a spoken direction into something on a map, or vice versa, I always have to stop and think twice to make sure I haven't got them backwards. I have some mnemonics, like "west rhymes with left", or mentally zooming the map out until I can see America and Russia (and I know which of _those_ is "the West"), but they're not instantaneous, and I always have to slow down to check them.

I'm convinced that this reversal in the default speech order is the reason. If my whole life I'd heard "west/east" and "left/right", I would have had no trouble matching up the one that comes first in both forms.

It especially annoys me when _I_ name the directions in those orders. After I've decided it's wrong and bad, you'd think I ought at least to be able to shake the habit myself! But I said 'east, west' again this morning without thinking and kicked myself.

items.title: I often find typos cognitively fascinating.
items.content:
I often find typos cognitively fascinating.

Some typos are just last-moment motor errors: "aimed for this key and hit the one next to it". Those are easy to understand. But others reveal much more interesting things about the mental process of driving your fingers on the keyboard, or even composing words.

I once aimed to type 'programs', and unexpectedly 'rpgroasm' came out. All the left-hand letters appear in the correct order, and so do all the right-hand letters, but they're interleaved in a spectacularly wrong way. That suggested that one part of my brain had sent an independent set of instructions to a subthing controlling each hand, and everything worked fine except the synchronisation between the two subthings.

There's another class of typo which I think of as 'brain got ahead of fingers': you're typing one word, but already thinking about a word that will come after it, and there's a crossover and you end up mixing up the two. Like 'bit bisect' in place of 'git bisect' – you're already planning the b, and it comes out of your fingers prematurely.

(Appropriately, as I typed _that_ sentence, 'in place' came out as 'pl inace', wow.)

Even the 'boring' motor errors have something cognitively interesting about them, just on the reading rather than writing side. We see 'adjacent letter on the keyboard' typos a lot, so our brains get good at correcting them. Sometimes _over_-correcting, so that you imagine a typo where none existed. When a sentence is a bit unexpected in context, I've been known to consider the possibility of a typo before figuring out how the sentence as originally spelled makes sense.

The best ones of those are when I hadn't even _realised_ the two words were a typo apart. I misread 'auction' as 'suction' once and it was a total surprise!

I wonder if there's any serious scholarly study of this kind of thing.

items.title: I had a really good afternoon at work yesterday.
items.content:
I had a really good afternoon at work yesterday.

I had a long pair-debugging session with a junior colleague, helping to track down a crash in something they were in the middle of writing. We started from the visible crash and backtracked to find the root cause, investigating everything along the way that looked odd.

We were expecting one bug, but ended up finding two. The load instruction that first put a bogus value into a register was loading from a totally wrong address, *and* there was some weird data at that address that shouldn't have been there, and those two wrong things had independent causes.

Neither bug by itself would have caused the crash: it needed both. If we'd found only one of them – for example by jumping to a conclusion, speculatively fixing something, and observing that the crash had gone away – then we'd have thought the whole problem was fixed, and been wrong. But by going through methodically to the point where the first weird thing happened, we were able to find both bugs. We fixed one on the spot, and ended the session knowing what to do about the other.

My colleague had asked for help with the aim of learning debugging skills (both low-level and general) as well as getting the bug fixed. I don't always have success when I do this on real-world problems, because if the problem turns out to be too hard, I can't solve it _and_ explain what I'm doing at the same time. Here, it was just about right: challenging, but not too much so.

I learned things too. We had to use LLDB rather than GDB, and I'm not nearly as familiar with LLDB, and now I'm more so. (It has a proper hex-dump command!) So it was a useful learning experience on both sides, as well as a successful bug-fixing exercise. They apologised afterwards for taking up my whole afternoon, but I think it was time well spent.

And to put the icing on the cake, nobody at any point suggested throwing an LLM at anything.

The only thing that bothers me about it is that this kind of experience is now rare enough in my life that I feel moved to toot about it when it happens!

Manpage Monday: bastille limits

Keep a noisy jail from eating the whole host. Powered by rctl + cpuset integrations.

Cap memory at 4G:> bastille limits myjail set memoryuse 4G

items.title: Moved our git web server from cgit to stagit to reduce load on the server caused by crawlers, as it only uses static files.
items.content:
Moved our git web server from cgit to stagit to reduce load on the server caused by crawlers, as it only uses static files.

Roughly 99.9% of requests are bots fetching commits and files over and over again at a rate of 50 req/s despite our robots.txt excluding any crawler. Stagit only exposes a small number of files and commits so they are not reachable to bots.

Sadly, many anti-bot protections rely on JS or fingerprinting which come with their own set of problems.

items.title: The most annoying ambiguity I can remember of that kind was the time I wanted to garbage-collect a PDF file: I had hand-edited it to remove a reference to one object in the file from another, and I wanted to make a smaller PDF with the now-unreferenced object completely removed.
items.content:
The most annoying ambiguity I can remember of that kind was the time I wanted to garbage-collect a PDF file: I had hand-edited it to remove a reference to one object in the file from another, and I wanted to make a smaller PDF with the now-unreferenced object completely removed.

If you search for "pdf garbage collection", you feel very foolish, because _all_ the hits are academic articles about garbage collection in general, published as PDFs.

(The answer to that one turns out to be "mutool clean".)

items.title: Got lucky with a web search just now.
items.content:
Got lucky with a web search just now.

I wanted to debug a crash in LLVM. For other programs I'd start by compiling with Address Sanitizer. LLVM's build process is tricky enough that you might not do that the obvious way, so I websearched "build llvm with address sanitizer".

Foolish me! That can also be interpreted as "build an LLVM toolchain that includes ASan for end users to use on the programs they build with it". Most of the hits were about that, and not about the thing I wanted.

But lucky me! I found a Stack Overflow post that recognised the ambiguity and answered _both_ questions. Top marks, that poster.

(The answer is "-DLLVM_USE_SANITIZER=Address".)
